title: Senior asks: a user saves the row {"name": "=HYPERLINK(\"http://evil.test\")"} to a CSV file. Later someone opens that file in Excel. What is the risk?
options: None: CSV is plain text, Excel shows it as it is
Excel treats the cell as a formula and runs it
json_encode blocks values that start with =
PHP refuses to write such a cell
explain: A cell that starts with =, +, - or @ can be run as a formula by Excel or Google Sheets. This is called CSV injection. Your API writes the value as it is, so the risk is real when files are downloaded. Fix: add a ' in front of such cells when writing, or reject them.

title: Senior asks: a client sends 600 nested lists [[[...]]] to write. decodeJson() uses json_decode($s, true). What does this print?
explain: json_decode has a default depth limit of 512. Deeper data is an error and the function returns null, without an exception. Your code then answers 'Invalid JSON.', which is a fair message. It is also a small protection against very deep input.

title: Senior asks: storage/ has fruits.csv. A user uploads Fruits.csv. On your Mac it gets the name Fruits_1.csv. On the Linux server it stays Fruits.csv. Why?
options: The Mac file system ignores case, so fopen('x') sees the same file
Linux changes names to lower case
The Mac adds _1 for every upload
explain: macOS (APFS) is case-insensitive by default, so Fruits.csv and fruits.csv are the same file and fopen with 'x' fails. Linux is case-sensitive, so they are two files. Same code, different result. Test on the system you deploy to, and decide if you want to compare names in lower case.

title: Log requests for debugging

pr.author: junior-dev
pr.title: Log requests for debugging
pr.body: I want to see what clients send. Now index.php logs every request body to the error log.

explain: The body is the content of the user's file. It can hold private data, and big uploads fill the log. Log the method, the action and the file name. Never log whole bodies, passwords or tokens. Also remember that user text in a log can fake extra log lines.

title: PHP 8. What does this print?
explain: ??= assigns only when the left side is missing or null. 0 is a real value, so x stays 0. y does not exist, so it gets 7. Do not confuse it with ?:, which also replaces 0, '' and false.

title: What does Node print?
explain: == treats null and undefined as equal, and as equal to nothing else, so null == 0 is false. But >= converts null to the number 0, so null >= 0 is true. Use === and check null with ?? or === null.

title: A trait with a static counter, used in two classes. What does this print?
explain: Every class that uses a trait gets its OWN copy of the static property. A and B do not share $n. B::inc() starts at 0 and gives 1. If you want one shared counter, keep it in a normal class and use that class from both.

title: A bug is in main now, but it was not there 100 commits ago. What is the fastest way to find the commit?
options: git bisect: mark good and bad, git checks the middle each time
git revert the last 100 commits one by one
git log -p and read all of it
explain: git bisect does a binary search. You mark one bad and one good commit. Git checks out the middle, you test and say good or bad, and repeat. 100 commits need only about 7 steps. Finish with git bisect reset.
